blocks.x: Milan Fashion Week concluded yesterday, following a whirlwind of spring-summer 2027 shows from marquee brands like Prada, Gucci, Jil Sander, and Bottega Veneta. Following the SS27 menswear presentations in June, these most recent presentations were primarily for the ladies, but—as is increasingly the case—there were still plenty of men’s looks in the mix. Among the week’s highlights were Glenn Martens’ farewell Diesel show, which sent off the Belgian designer in a (literal) orgy of denim speedos and freaky leathers, as well as front-row appearances by fashion-loving celebrities including Travis Scott, Jacob Elordi, and Naomi Osaka.

As a showcase of spring-summer 2027 designs, Milan Fashion Week’s collections don’t just preview what the world’s elite retailers will be selling next year—they also suggest how those clothes might influence the rest of the fashion pantheon. That means whether you’re shopping the racks at Prada or scrolling your feed for inspo, the runways had plenty to get your wheels turning. Here are a few of the key trends we saw, along with advice on how to integrate them into your wardrobe.

It’s no secret that precision layering is the keystone of many an elite fit, but this season’s shows pushed the idea far beyond its conventional boundaries. Much of this was for theatrical effect (showing off as many clothes as possible is also likely a factor), but anyone who takes the art of layering seriously should take note, as there’s much to learn. At Ferragamo, for instance, one of the show's strongest looks featured a utility vest over a white button-up shirt and tie, tucked into wide, cream-colored trousers, a combination that’s both counterintuitive and extremely vibey. Marni tried something similar with a vest over a sleeveless dress shirt and tie, and it might be the best cure yet invented for a case of the Mondays. Gucci’s overcoat-hoodie-dress-shirt-turtleneck combo is more of a swing, but—as with many ideas that appear on the runway—it’s as much inspo as instruction. As such, if there’s one takeaway from all of the kooky layering we saw in Milan, it’s that wherever you’re at in your layering journey, the only limit is your appetite for experimentation.

Pattern and color mixing is right up there with layering among the high arts of style, and designers really went for it this season with all manner of strange and wonderful mashups. Among the most cheerful of these appeared on the Marni runway in a look that combined a rainbow fair isle-style sweater, a black-and-tan color-blocked overcoat, and some tan shorts with an embossed grid pattern. If there’s a mathematical formula for combining shapes, colors, and patterns, it's here. Another equally moodboardable Marni look paired a cobalt blue cardigan and a butter yellow button-up shirt with a tie, jacket, and trousers in soft, earthy hues. Meanwhile at Gucci, a monogram belt was the cherry on top of an outfit that included a striped rugby worn over a striped button-up. If you were in need of any further evidence that quiet luxury is on the way out, here it is. Also, if you’re looking to try your hand at power-clashing, a micro-striped shirt beneath the fat bars of a classic rugby is an easy place to start.

Ever since the first cowboy paired a denim shirt with his favorite dungarees, denim-on-denim has been among the most reliable ways to pop off in absolute comfort. It’s no surprise, then, that it continues to resonate with designers, the latest of which are Silvana Armani and Leo Dell’Orco, who peppered their latest Emporio Armani collection (and last before Dario Vitale takes over next season) with lightweight denim in a palette of washed-out grays and crisp blacks. There were overcoats, trench coats, and—of course—a whole lot of jeans, but the best look of the bunch was a deconstructed three-piece denim suit that brings new meaning to the term “Canadian Tuxedo.” The key takeaways here are that a) denim remains the most versatile fabric ever created and b) the frontiers of denim-on-denim extend far beyond those age-old cowboy standbys.

Milan’s runways offered a timely counterpoint to all the baggy, billowy, wide-cut trousers we’ve seen of late, with a parade of crisp, slim (but not skinny) tailored bottoms. The colors ranged from black, gray, and navy to earthy shades of olive green, terra cotta, and deep brown, and the fabrics were equally diverse, but they all shared a similar level of tailored tidiness. So does that mean wide trousers are cooked? We don’t think so. Instead—and in keeping with the pluralism of the menswear moment—you can choose your team or say yes to both.

Leather jackets have been an essential part of the outerwear pantheon since prehistoric times, but the assortment has never been so broad. Likewise, leather pants made a strong showing on Milan’s runways, courtesy of Diesel (whose distressed blue versions and matching jacket were Avatar-esque in the best sense), Bottega, and Ferragamo, among many others. Marni had a pair in a deep cocoa brown that looked as comfy as a well-worn pair of five-pocket jeans, but even more alluring was the brand’s trim blazer-bomber hybrid in black leather with notch lapels and elastic cuffs. Everyone looks good in a leather jacket—that’s just facts, but leather pants are a tougher hang by orders of magnitude. This year’s collections suggest now might be the best time in years to give ‘em a go. After all, if Tom Brady can get on the cowhide trouser train, you can too.
